subject: B4480B0CDB52EF0534E437134978DC1E
introduction: These readings, most of them prayers, say one thing in many settings: that power belongs to God, who was before all things, created by a word, does what He wills, humbles the mighty and raises the lowly, cannot be frustrated, and is sovereign even in a Messenger who is a prisoner. A hundred of the guide's three hundred quotations are read here, in the proportions of its thirteen sections, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside, and many are their close kin: the psalms, Isaiah, Job, Daniel's kings, the Magnificat, the Qur'an's 'Be! and it is', Paul. Ten push back or add a side: Socrates asks whether the good is good because God wills it, Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth shall not do right, Habakkuk asks how long, Machiavelli counts the fate of unarmed prophets, and Jesus in Gethsemane and before Pilate shows what such power looks like in a human life.
questions: The readings say that God does whatsoever He wills. Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth shall not do right, and Socrates whether the good is good because it is willed. How do the readings hold power and justice together?
Several readings speak of a sovereignty shown in a prisoner without armies. What kind of power is that, and how does Machiavelli's remark about unarmed prophets look in its light?
'None can frustrate His purpose': Habakkuk asks how long he must cry unheard. How do you live in the time between the claim and its evidence?
Many of these readings are prayers ending 'Potent art Thou to do what pleaseth Thee'. What does that refrain do to the request that came before it?
Daniel's kings, Isaiah's princes and Shelley's Ozymandias all fall. What is a person or a nation asked to learn from the passing of earthly rule?

outside.why: The psalm says: before the mountains were brought forth, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
Isaiah has the Lord say: I am the first, and I am the last, and beside me there is no God.
Malachi has God say in five words what the reading says at length: I am the Lord, I change not.
The Revelation has the Lord say: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, the Almighty.
The psalm says that the heavens shall perish and wax old like a garment, but thou shalt endure.
Daniel foretells a kingdom set up by the God of heaven which shall never be destroyed nor left to other people.
Shelley's traveller reads on a broken statue the boast of a king of kings, and round it the lone and level sands stretch far away.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
Genesis tells the first act of creation in one sentence: and God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
The Qur'an says that His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is.
The psalm says: he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
The psalm says that the heavens declare the glory of God, and that day unto day uttereth speech.
The letter to the Hebrews speaks of one upholding all things by the word of his power.
Isaiah has God say: I form the light, and create darkness; I make peace, and create evil. If light is brought from fire and joy from sorrow, is the fire and the sorrow also His work?
Paul writes of God: of him, and through him, and to him, are all things, to whom be glory for ever.
John's Gospel says that all things were made by the Word, and without him was not any thing made that was made.
Paul asks: hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
Isaiah asks: shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?

Plato's Socrates asks whether the holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods. If the excellence of all things depends on God's bidding, could cruelty have been made excellent?
Jesus says: with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
The angel tells Mary that with God nothing shall be impossible, and she answers: be it unto me according to thy word.
King Nebuchadnezzar, restored to his reason, says that God doeth according to his will, and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
Job, having lost everything, says: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
Paul quotes what was said to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.
In Exodus God tells Moses: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy.
The Qur'an calls God the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who saith unto a thing only: Be! and it is.
God answers Job out of the whirlwind: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?
Hannah sings that the Lord maketh poor and maketh rich, bringeth low and lifteth up, and raiseth up the poor out of the dust.
Mary sings that God hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
Isaiah says of God that he bringeth the princes to nothing, and maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.
Isaiah says that the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance.
The psalm says: put not your trust in princes, whose breath goeth forth and whose thoughts perish in that very day.
Paul says that God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Shakespeare's Richard says that within the hollow crown that rounds the mortal temples of a king, Death keeps his court.
God proclaims himself to Moses as merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.

Habakkuk cries: O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? If God is supreme over his servants, what is the believer to make of the time during which the proof is ignored and nothing happens?
Abraham dares to ask God: shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Is it a limit on sovereignty that it should be answerable to justice, or is that what equity means?
John sees the dead, small and great, stand before God, and the books opened, and the dead judged.
Matthew says that the people were astonished at Jesus's teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Mark tells how Jesus rebuked the wind and said unto the sea, Peace, be still, and there was a great calm.
John tells how Jesus cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth, and he that was dead came forth.
The risen Jesus says to his disciples: all power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.
Paul writes of Christ that in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Paul writes that God hath given him a name which is above every name, at which every knee should bow.
The Qur'an tells of the trumpet blown, at which all who are in the heavens and the earth swoon away.
Daniel is told that the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end.
Isaiah has God say that the word that goeth forth out of his mouth shall not return unto him void.
Jeremiah hears: before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Jesus says: I can of mine own self do nothing; I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me. How do complete power and complete dependence belong to the same person?
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
Jesus, a prisoner before Pilate, says: my kingdom is not of this world, or else would my servants fight.
Paul says of Christ that he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Acts tells how Paul and Silas, in prison at midnight, prayed and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them.
The psalm says that the kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord, and he that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh.
Gamaliel warns the council: if this work be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
Proverbs says that there is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the Lord.
Isaiah says that the Lord's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear.
Job says at the end: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
Paul asks the Romans: what shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?
The Qur'an says that they would put out the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light.
Jesus says that he will build his church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Machiavelli drew the opposite lesson from history: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. What counts as not being frustrated, when a cause has no arms?
Daniel reads the writing on the wall to a king at his feast: God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.
While the boast was still in the king's mouth, a voice from heaven said: the kingdom is departed from thee.
The psalm warns: be wise now therefore, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Kipling, at the height of empire, wrote that all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
Isaiah addresses a fallen king: how art thou fallen from heaven, who didst weaken the nations!
Proverbs says that the king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Ezekiel has God promise: a new heart will I give you, and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh.
Jesus gives the same ground for obedience in a sentence: if ye love me, keep my commandments.
In the Revelation Christ says: behold, I stand at the door, and knock; if any man open the door, I will come in. What kind of dominion over the heart waits to be let in?
The psalm says that God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
The psalm promises: thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night, nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness.
The psalm blesses the Lord who forgiveth all thine iniquities and healeth all thy diseases.
In Exodus God says to the people in the wilderness: I am the Lord that healeth thee.
James tells the sick to call for the elders, who pray and anoint with oil, and says that the prayer of faith shall save the sick.
The psalmist says: the Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
The psalmist says that if he take the wings of the morning, even there shall thy hand lead him.
The psalmist cries: out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice.
David prays: thine, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty.
The Qur'an's Throne verse says that His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and that He is never weary of preserving them.
Habakkuk says: the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.
John hears the voice of a great multitude, as the voice of many waters, saying: Alleluia, for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
The Lord's Prayer ends with the same refrain: thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever.
The Qur'an tells of those who, warned that the people had gathered against them, only grew in faith and said that God is sufficient for them.
Tennyson's dying Arthur says that more things are wrought by prayer than this world dreams of.
Jeremiah prays: thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power, and there is nothing too hard for thee.
The psalm says: commit thy way unto the Lord; trust also in him, and he shall bring it to pass.
Isaiah asks: hast thou not known that the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?
In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup may pass, and adds: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. What does a prayer to the All-Powerful sound like when the answer may be no?
Moses's blessing says: the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.
Paul ends a prayer: now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think.
The psalm says: twice have I heard this, that power belongeth unto God; also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy.
When Sarah laughs at the promise of a child, God asks: is any thing too hard for the Lord?
Paul quotes a call to the sleeper: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

Emerson called prayer that craves a particular commodity vicious, and prayer as a means to a private end meanness and theft. Does the refrain 'Powerful art Thou to do what Thou pleasest' ask for something, or give something up?
Isaiah has God say: there is none that can deliver out of my hand; I will work, and who shall let it?
The Qur'an has God say: I am nigh; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.
James says: ye have not, because ye ask not; ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss. If God can do what He wills, what makes one request fit to bring to Him and another not?
The psalm says that he that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.

daniel-none-can-stay-his-hand.text: I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou

proverbs-no-counsel-against-the-lord.text: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the Lord. The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the Lord

job-thou-canst-do-every-thing.text: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee. Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not

proverbs-kings-heart.text: The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will

jeremiah-nothing-too-hard.text: Ah Lord God! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee

ephesians-exceeding-abundantly.text: Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end

revelation-lord-god-omnipotent.text: And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth

genesis-any-thing-too-hard.text: Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old? Is any thing too hard for the Lord? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son

isaiah-who-shall-let-it.text: Yea, before the day was I am he; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand: I will work, and who shall let it

psalm-power-belongeth-unto-god.text: God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God. Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy: for thou renderest to every man according to his work

psalm-he-that-sitteth-in-the-heavens.text: The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying, Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us. He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision
